paragraphs: A body politic can be measured in two ways, by the extent of its territory or by the number of its people, and there is a right relation between these two measures that makes a State truly great. Men make the State, and the land sustains the men. The right relation, therefore, is that the land should suffice to maintain its inhabitants, and that there should be as many inhabitants as the land can maintain. In this proportion lies the _maximum_ strength of a given number of people. For if there is too much land, it is troublesome to guard, poorly cultivated and produces more than is needed, and this soon gives rise to defensive wars; if there is too little, the State depends on its neighbors for what it lacks, and this soon gives rise to offensive wars. Any people whose situation leaves it no choice except between commerce and war is weak in itself. It depends on its neighbors and on circumstances, and its existence can never be more than short and uncertain. It either conquers others and changes its situation, or it is conquered and becomes nothing. Only insignificance or greatness can keep it free.

No fixed relation can be stated between the extent of territory and the size of population that suit each other. This is partly because of differences in the quality and fertility of the land, in the nature of its products and in the influence of climate, and partly because of the different temperaments of the inhabitants: some in a fertile country consume little, and others on a poor soil consume much. One must also take into account how fertile the women are, which conditions in each country favor or hinder the growth of population, and how much influence the legislator can hope to have through his institutions. The legislator should therefore go not by what he sees but by what he foresees, and should stop not so much at the population he actually finds as at the one it ought naturally to reach. Lastly, there are countless cases in which particular local circumstances call for, or allow, the acquisition of more territory than seems necessary. Thus a people will expand widely in a mountainous country, where the natural products, _i.e._ woods and pastures, need less labor, where experience shows that women are more fertile than on the plains, and where a great expanse of slope yields only a small level area that can be counted on for crops. On the other hand, a people can contract on the coast, even in lands of rocks and nearly barren sands, because there fishing makes up to a great extent for the lack of land produce, because the inhabitants have to gather closer together to repel pirates, and also because it is easier to relieve the country of its surplus inhabitants by means of colonies.

To these conditions for giving laws must be added one more which, though it cannot take the place of the others, makes them all useless when it is missing: the enjoyment of peace and plenty. For the moment when a State sets its house in order is like the moment when a battalion is forming up: its body is then least able to resist and easiest to destroy. Resistance would be better in a time of complete disorganization than at a moment of ferment, when everyone is occupied with his own position and not with the danger. If war, famine or sedition arises in this time of crisis, the State will inevitably be overthrown.

It is not that many governments have not been set up during such storms; but in those cases the governments themselves destroy the State. Usurpers always bring about or choose troubled times to pass, under cover of public terror, destructive laws that the people would never adopt in cold blood. The moment chosen is one of the surest ways of telling the work of the legislator from that of the tyrant.

What people, then, is fit to receive laws? One that is already bound together by some unity of origin, interest or convention, but has never yet felt the real yoke of law. One that has neither customs nor superstitions deeply rooted. One that has no fear of being overwhelmed by a sudden invasion. One that, without entering into its neighbors’ quarrels, can resist each of them single-handed, or get the help of one to repel another. One in which every member can be known by every other, and there is no need to lay on any man a burden too heavy for a man to bear. One that can do without other peoples, and without which all other peoples can do;[1] one that is neither rich nor poor but self-sufficient; and, lastly, one that unites the stability of an ancient people with the docility of a new one. Legislation is made difficult less by what must be built up than by what must be destroyed, and what makes success so rare is the impossibility of finding natural simplicity together with the needs of society. All these conditions are indeed rarely found together, and therefore few States have good constitutions.

There is still one country in Europe capable of being given laws: Corsica. The valor and persistence with which that brave people has regained and defended its liberty well deserve that some wise man teach it how to preserve what it has won. I have a feeling that some day that little island will astonish Europe.

The Republic of Thlascala, enclosed within the Mexican Empire, preferred to do without salt rather than buy it from the Mexicans, or even receive it from them as a gift. The Thlascalans were wise enough to see the snare hidden under such generosity. They kept their freedom, and that little State, shut up inside that great Empire, was finally the instrument of its ruin.
